question: A 15-year-old adolescent presents to his pediatrician with progressive easy fatigability and exercises intolerance over the last several months. The patient was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. There is no history of palpitation, dyspnea, or lower limb edema. On physical examination his vital signs are stable. On chest auscultation, a wide fixed split in the second heart sound is detected. A medium-pitched systolic ejection murmur is present which is best heard at the left middle and upper sternal border. A short mid-diastolic rumble is also audible over the lower left sternal border, which is best heard with the bell of the stethoscope. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present on this patient’s echocardiogram?

options.opb: Anterior movement of ventricular septum during systole
options.opc: Goose-neck deformity of left ventricular outflow tract
options.ope: Displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets inferiorly into right ventricle

enhanced_information: The 15-year-old patient presents with symptoms suggestive of an atrial septal defect (ASD), characterized by easy fatigability and exercise intolerance. The wide fixed split of the second heart sound and the presence of a systolic ejection murmur indicate increased blood flow to the right heart, leading to right ventricular volume overload. This condition typically results in right ventricular dilation and can cause displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets inferiorly into the right ventricle. The reasoning chains consistently point to this finding, supported by the consensus that ASDs lead to right heart changes due to increased blood flow. Therefore, the most likely echocardiographic finding in this patient is the displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets inferiorly into the right ventricle.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 15-year-old patient, including easy fatigability, exercise intolerance, a wide fixed split of the second heart sound, and a systolic ejection murmur, is highly suggestive of an atrial septal defect (ASD). In ASD, there is increased blood flow to the right heart, leading to right ventricular volume overload. This condition typically results in right ventricular dilation and can cause the tricuspid valve leaflets to be displaced inferiorly into the right ventricle due to the increased volume. The other options do not align with the expected echocardiographic findings associated with ASD. Therefore, the most likely echocardiographic finding in this patient is the displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets inferiorly into the right ventricle, which is consistent with the known pathophysiology of ASD. Thus, the best-supported option is 'ope'.
